To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the effects of aptitude on learning depend on the instructional method and (2) these interactions can be predicted from a theory of learning and instruction.

(a) the individual-difference variable is the student, (b) the instructional variable is instruction, (c) the outcome variable is student learning, (d) the research design is formative, (e) the research strategy is experimental, (f) the research method is the classroom laboratory, and (g) the research goal is to improve the effectiveness of instruction.
the failure of aptitude-treatment-interaction research to be practically applicable in designing instruction does not justify ignoring individual differences in designing instruction.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of individual difference variables that have a demonstrable effect on instruction and learning, and the development of instructional methods that capitalize on the effect of individual differences.
the development of an individualized instructional system based on the notion that the most important aspect of individual difference is the uniqueness of the individual.
the identification of individual difference characteristics that are relevant to instruction and with the identification of methods of instructional design that are responsive to these differences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the failure of aptitude-treatment research to produce practical applications is not an argument for ignoring individual difference.
individual differences should be considered in instructional design, and that formative evaluation is a useful approach to doing so.
the ATI model is not the appropriate one to accommodate individual differences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have found no reason to expect individual differences in the way they have been studied to be of much use to the instructional designer in the design of instruction, but that we do have reason to believe that individual differences can be studied so as to provide the designer with useful information.
the current ATI approach is not useful in accommodating individual differences, and a formative approach is more promising.

we are not yet able to design individualized instruction for individual students, and that we are not even close to designing instruction that will accommodate the individual differences that we have been able to identify and quantify.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the failure of the ATI approach to be practically useful is not due to a lack of attention to individual difference, but rather due to a lack attention to individual uniqueness
individual differences are not just a problem to be solved, but rather an opportunity to be exploited in the design of instruction and assessment.
the failure of the aptitude-treatment research to be practically helpful in instruction design does not justify ignoring individual differences.
